name: Kira Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Kira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo underground at the gold mine. A jumbo is a drill rig with two long arms, booms, and I drill the face, the end of the tunnel, in a pattern so the charge-up crew can load it and blast it. A good shift is three faces drilled clean with no stuck rods. I've got an AI app on my phone that I use every day, for everything from checking a drill pattern question to writing listings for my side business.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the side business, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I fix up old ride-on mowers and small engines in our shed and sell them online, maybe two or three a month. It started as a hobby and now it pays for the kids' sport. What wears me out is the hours and the money. My husband Jake works part-time at the farm supply store, we've got Ruby, who's 12, and Owen, who's 9, and a mortgage on five acres just out of town. I'm on the lower operator rate because I only got my jumbo ticket three years ago, after years as a nipper, the person who runs supplies underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it was oversold, but the tools still save me time. I'd post something like that in the local small business group. People who use them well will still get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. I've already got AI helping me with the mower business, and if nothing radical happens, I keep my mine job and grow the shed on the side. That's the plan anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working at the mine and push the mower business to four or five sales a month. I'd use the AI to price parts and write better ads. If it kept growing, I'd look at a small business loan for a proper workshop in a couple of years, maybe $15,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Calm, a bit itchy to grow the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the AI help with the mower business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take a photo of a busted carburettor and ask it what's wrong, and nine times out of ten it's right. Then I ask it to write the ad and suggest a price. It's like having a mate who knows small engines and never gets tired of my questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow $15,000 with thin savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the numbers worked. I'd want a year of steady sales first. Jake's more careful than me, he'd make me show him on paper, and he'd be right to.

S0.say: She'd say it was oversold but the tools still save time, posting this in the local small business group. People who use them well will still get ahead.
S0.think: It suits her: she keeps the mine job and grows her mower repair business on the side with AI help.
S0.do: Keeps working and pushes the mower business to four or five sales a month using AI for pricing and ads. Considers a $15,000 business loan for a workshop in a couple of years if sales hold steady.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit eager to grow the business.
S0.quote: It's like having a mate who knows small engines and never gets tired of my questions.
S0.fieldNote: She sees AI as a working tool for her side business, not a threat. Her traditional outlook shows in self-reliance and building something her family owns. Her husband acts as the cautious check on her appetite for risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to back yourself. I'd tell people at the mine to learn the new gear and think about something on the side, because no one's going to hand you a future. And I'd say the government should stay out of the way of small businesses trying to adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm in good shape. Jumbos are already going semi-automatic, and someone has to supervise them from the surface. Plus I've got the shed. Two legs to stand on is better than one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first few months I'd put my hand up to run the semi-automatic jumbo trial and learn the system. I'd grow the mower business to a steady $1,000 a month and start putting half of that into savings. By the end of year one I'd want three months of savings for the first time ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a buzz. I like a challenge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The nippers and the young blokes on the charge-up crew. Those are the jobs that can go without much fuss, and a lot of them are just out of school. I'd tell them to get a trade or a ticket now, before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Jake say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say slow down, you can't do everything. He's probably right. But he'd also be the one picking up mower parts in town for me.

S1.say: She'd say it's time to back yourself and urge people at the mine to learn new gear and start something on the side. She'd want government to stay out of the way of small businesses adapting.
S1.think: She thinks she's in good shape, since someone must supervise semi-automatic jumbos from the surface and she has her side business too.
S1.do: Volunteers early for the semi-automatic jumbo trial to learn the system. Grows the mower business to $1,000 a month and saves half, aiming for three months of savings by the end of year one.
S1.feel: Calm with a buzz of excitement at the challenge.
S1.quote: Two legs to stand on is better than one.
S1.fieldNote: She is confident because she has both a path at the mine and a business of her own. Her free-market outlook shows in wanting government to stay out of the way. Her concern for young workers is practical: get a trade or a ticket now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to get busy, not wait for a handout. But honestly I'd also say this is too fast, and somebody needs to make sure it doesn't wreck every country town at once. I'd say that even though I don't usually want the government in my business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. If robots can drill the face and also fix a mower, then both my legs go at once. And with how little we've got saved, two years isn't a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd sell what I can from the shed and stockpile cash, maybe $8,000 if I push hard. I'd use the AI to find any jobs where people still want a person, like local repairs for older folks who won't trust a robot. When it arrived, I'd lean on Jake's family and the community and try to stay useful any way I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep moving because that's how I cope, but I'd be scared underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grab cash and get the shed paid off, not much else. You can't build a new business that beats a robot in two years. You can only make sure you're not broke when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction between not wanting handouts and asking for help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, there is, and I know it. I'd still rather earn it. But if every job in town goes in the same month, it's not about people being lazy anymore.

S2.say: She'd say people need to get busy rather than wait for handouts, but also that this is too fast and someone must stop it wrecking every country town. She'd say it despite usually wanting government out of her business.
S2.think: If robots can drill the face and fix mowers, both her income sources go at once. With so little saved, two years isn't much.
S2.do: Sells shed stock and builds up about $8,000 cash in the two years before. Uses AI to find work where people still want a person, such as repairs for older locals, and leans on her husband's family and the community once it arrives.
S2.feel: Alarmed; keeps moving to cope but is scared underneath.
S2.quote: But if every job in town goes in the same month, it's not about people being lazy anymore.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture knocks out both of her income streams at once, which is what makes it different for her. She openly owned the contradiction between her dislike of handouts and her call for help. She copes by staying busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get a plan going if you start today. I'd tell everyone I know to work out what they can own or fix that people will still pay a person for. And I'd want the council to make it easier to run a small business from home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me a real shot, but it's tight with no savings. I'd be 48. I'd want to have the workshop running and paid off before 2031, so I own something when the mine job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get a small business loan, maybe $15,000, for a proper workshop, and use the AI to run the books and the ads. I'd stay at the mine as long as possible to keep the wage coming. By year three I'd want the shed bringing in enough to cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a good way, mostly. Like the first day on a new rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just said 'no savings' and 'loan' in the same breath. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. But the money's no good in the bank if the job's gone by 2031. I'd rather put it into something I own. Jake would want to see the numbers first, and I'd show him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the workshop survive once AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not forever. But for a few years, people out here will still want someone they know to fix their stuff. I'd bet on that.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to start a plan today and urge people to find something they can own or fix that people will still pay a person for. She'd want the council to make home businesses easier.
S3.think: Five years gives her a real shot but is tight without savings. She wants the workshop running and paid off before 2031 so she owns something when the mine job goes.
S3.do: Takes a $15,000 small business loan in year one for a proper workshop, using AI for books and ads. Stays at the mine to keep the wage and aims for the shed to cover the mortgage by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but mostly in a good way, like the first day on a new rig.
S3.quote: But the money's no good in the bank if the job's gone by 2031. I'd rather put it into something I own.
S3.fieldNote: With five years she is willing to borrow against thin savings to own something, and she defends it clearly. Her trust in local, face-to-face service is her bet against automation. Her husband's caution remains the check on her plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't use it is wasting it. I'd say families and towns should plan together, and the government should keep red tape off small operators. I'd be upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels pretty good. I'd be 53, the kids would be grown, and I could build the workshop properly and maybe hire a young apprentice. The only thing that worries me is whether people will still want a person in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the shed slowly for a few years, then take the loan around year three or four once the numbers are solid. I'd move to the surface jumbo control room when it's offered. And I'd teach Ruby and Owen how to fix things, because owning a skill matters more than owning a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small question mark. It feels like time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hire an apprentice if robots are coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone taught me. The old jumbo driver, Bruce, spent two years showing me how to read the ground. I'd want to pass that on while it still counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between five and ten years for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five I'd be borrowing and hoping. With ten I can build it properly and only borrow when the numbers are solid. That's a big difference when you've got nothing saved.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty and shouldn't be wasted, with families and towns planning together and government keeping red tape off small operators.
S4.think: Ten years feels good: at 53 with grown kids she could build the workshop properly and maybe hire an apprentice. Her only worry is whether people will still want a person in 2036.
S4.do: Grows the shed business slowly, taking the loan around year three or four once the numbers are solid. Moves to the surface jumbo control room when offered and teaches her children to fix things.
S4.feel: Mostly fine with a small question mark; time to build something.
S4.quote: Because someone taught me. The old jumbo driver, Bruce, spent two years showing me how to read the ground.
S4.fieldNote: Time lets her slow down and borrow only when it's safe, which she says matters most with no savings. Her wish to train an apprentice comes from gratitude to the man who trained her. She values owning a skill over owning a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It takes out the mine and the shed at the same time, and we don't have the money to wait it out. What would help is fewer hoops for small businesses, cheap loans for people starting something useful in their own town, and a short-term safety net for families while they find their feet, because a crash that fast isn't anyone's fault.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they can fix. Everyone asks what job they do. I think the better question now is what do you know how to fix, because that's what people will still pay for.

headlineQuote: I'd teach Ruby and Owen how to fix things, because owning a skill matters more than owning a job.
portrait: Kira Abbott is a 43-year-old underground jumbo drill operator at a gold mine who worked her way up from supply runner and uses AI tools every day. She and her husband, who works part-time at a farm supply store, have two children, a mortgage on five acres and almost no savings, but she runs a growing mower repair business from her shed. She believes in self-reliance and small business and wants government out of the way, though she admits the two-year AGI picture is too fast for that to hold. With more time she would build a proper workshop and pass her skills on, as an old jumbo driver once did for her.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it takes out both her mine job and her repair business at once and the family can't wait it out.
whatWouldHelp: Fewer hoops and cheap loans for small businesses in their own towns, plus a short-term safety net for families while they find their feet.
